questions.q: The components of the spine are:
opts: Musculoskeletal: vertebral column; Neurological: spinal cord + spinal nerves
questions.exp: Spine components: musculoskeletal: vertebral column; neurological: spinal cord + spinal nerves. (Book p173)

questions.q: The vertebrae are classified as:
questions.exp: Vertebrae: cervical (C), thoracic (T)/dorsal (D), lumbar (L), sacral (S). (Book p173)

questions.q: The intervertebral disc is made of:
questions.exp: Intervertebral disc: annulus fibrosus and nucleus pulposus. (Book p173)

questions.q: The functions of the intervertebral disc include:
opts: Segments the spine (increased mobility) and acts as a shock absorber
questions.exp: Functions: segments the spine (increased mobility); shock absorber. (Book p173)

questions.q: A fracture of the pars inter-articularis is called:
questions.exp: Pars inter-articularis: fracture (spondylolysis) -> spondylolisthesis (slipping of one vertebra over another). (Book p173)

questions.q: Spondylolisthesis means:
opts: Slipping of one vertebra over another
questions.exp: Spondylolisthesis: slipping of one vertebra over another. (Book p173)

questions.q: The articular facets articulate to:
questions.exp: Articular facets: articulates to keep the spine aligned. (Book p173)

questions.q: Denis' concept of spine stability is based on:
questions.exp: Denis' concept of spine stability: based on 3 columns of vertebra. (Book p173)

questions.q: The anterior column of the spine includes:
opts: Anterior longitudinal ligament, anterior annulus, anterior 2/3rd of vertebral body
questions.exp: Anterior column: anterior longitudinal ligament, anterior annulus, anterior 2/3rd of vertebral body. (Book p173)

questions.q: The middle column of the spine includes:
opts: Posterior 1/3rd of vertebral body, posterior annulus, posterior longitudinal ligament
questions.exp: Middle column: posterior 1/3rd of vertebral body, posterior annulus, posterior longitudinal ligament. (Book p173)

questions.q: The posterior column of the spine includes:
opts: Posterior elements (pedicles, facets, lamina, spinous process) and posterior ligaments
questions.exp: Posterior column: posterior elements (pedicles, facets, lamina, spinous process); posterior ligaments. (Book p173)

questions.q: An injury involving only 1 column of the spine is:
questions.exp: Clinical aspect: injury involving 1 column -> stable injury; Rx: conservative. (Book p174)

questions.q: An injury involving 2 or more columns of the spine is:
questions.exp: Injury involving 2 or more columns -> unstable injury; Rx: stabilization / fixation (surgery). (Book p174)

questions.q: The m/c site of vertebral fracture is:
questions.exp: M/c site: vertebral fracture: lower thoracic (T12). (Book p174)

questions.q: The m/c site of vertebral dislocation is the:
questions.exp: M/c site: vertebral dislocation: cervical spine. (Book p174)

questions.q: The cervical spine is prone to dislocation d/t:
opts: Ligamentous stabilizers > bony, and horizontal arrangement of articular facets
questions.exp: Cervical spine d/t: stabilizers: ligamentous > bony; horizontal arrangement of articular facets. (Book p174)

questions.q: The lumbar spine has a vertical arrangement of articular facets, which gives:
questions.exp: Lumbar spine: vertical arrangement of articular facets -> increased risk of fracture > dislocation. (Book p174)

questions.q: The highest risk of spinal cord injury is with:
questions.exp: Highest risk of spinal cord injury: cervical spine fracture. (Book p174)

questions.q: Immediate management in cervical spine injury is:
opts: Turn patient onto their back, support placed behind neck, transported to nearest hospital
questions.exp: Note: 1. turn patient onto their back; 2. support placed behind neck; 3. transported to nearest hospital. (Book p174)

questions.q: Jefferson's fracture is the m/c fracture of the:
questions.exp: Jefferson's / C1 vertebral (atlas) fracture: m/c fracture on C1 vertebra. (Book p175)

questions.q: The mechanism of injury in Jefferson's fracture is:
opts: Axial loading / compression - fragments burst out away from spinal canal
questions.exp: Mechanism of injury: axial loading / compression; fragments burst out away from spinal canal. (Book p175)

questions.q: A characteristic feature of Jefferson's fracture is:
questions.exp: Jefferson's fracture: no neurological deficits. (Book p175)

questions.q: Investigations in Jefferson's fracture include:
opts: X-ray (open mouth view) and CT scan (best)
questions.exp: Investigations: X-ray (open mouth view); CT scan (best). (Book p175)

questions.q: A stable Jefferson's fracture is treated:
questions.exp: Treatment: stable fracture: conservative. (Book p175)

questions.q: An unstable Jefferson's fracture (torn transverse ligament) is treated with:
questions.exp: Unstable: surgery (atlanto-occipital fusion). (Book p175)

questions.q: The types of C2 vertebral (axis) fracture are:
opts: Odontoid fracture (m/c fracture of C2) and Hangman's fracture
questions.exp: Types: odontoid fracture: m/c fracture of C2; Hangman's fracture. (Book p175)

questions.q: Hangman's fracture is a fracture of the:
opts: Pars inter-articularis of C2 vertebra (spondylolysis of C2)
questions.exp: Hangman's fracture: fracture of pars inter-articularis of C2 vertebra (spondylolysis of C2). (Book p175)

questions.q: Hangman's fracture causes:
questions.exp: Hangman's fracture causes dislocation of C2 over C3 (spondylolisthesis). (Book p175)

questions.q: In Hangman's fracture, the neurological status is typically:
questions.exp: Hangman's fracture: no neurological deficit. (Book p175)

questions.q: The m/c cause of Hangman's fracture is:
questions.exp: M/c cause: RTA > hanging. (Book p175)

questions.q: Whiplash injury is a:
questions.exp: Whiplash injury: soft tissue injury. (Book p175)

questions.q: The mechanism of whiplash injury is:
questions.exp: Mechanism: hyperextension -> flexion. (Book p175)

questions.q: Features of whiplash injury include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Features: chronic neck pain; no neurological deficits; normal X-ray / CT scan. (Book p175)

questions.q: Treatment of whiplash injury is:
questions.exp: Rx: cervical collar. (Book p175)

questions.q: Clay Shoveler's fracture results from shoveling with strong contraction of paraspinal and upper limb muscles, causing:
questions.exp: Clay Shoveler's fracture: shoveling -> strong contraction of paraspinal and upper limb muscles -> avulsion of C7 spinous process. (Book p176)

questions.q: The Chance (jack-knife / seat-belt) fracture was described by:
questions.exp: Chance / jack-knife / seat-belt fracture: described by Dr. G.G. Chance. (Book p176)

questions.q: In Chance fracture, a complete transverse splitting of the vertebra is called:
questions.exp: Complete transverse splitting of: vertebra: bony Chance; ligament and disc: soft tissue Chance. (Book p176)

questions.q: The mechanism of injury in Chance fracture is:
opts: Seatbelts without shoulder harnesses -> flexion of spine at lumbar vertebra -> complete transection of spinal cord (involves all 3 columns: unstable fracture) -> paraplegia
questions.exp: Mechanism: seatbelts without shoulder harnesses; flexion of spine at lumbar vertebra; complete transection of spinal cord (involves all 3 columns: unstable fracture); paraplegia. (Book p176)

questions.q: Treatment of Chance fracture is:
questions.exp: Rx: stabilization and surgery. (Book p176)

questions.q: The causative factor of a compression fracture is:
questions.exp: Causative factor: compression fracture: osteoporosis. (Book p176)

questions.q: The causative factor of a burst fracture is:
questions.exp: Causative factor: burst fracture: significant trauma. (Book p176)

questions.q: The mechanism of a compression fracture is:
questions.exp: Mechanism: compression fracture: flexion -> compression. (Book p176)

questions.q: The mechanism of a burst fracture is:
questions.exp: Mechanism: burst fracture: axial loading. (Book p176)

questions.q: The characteristic feature of a compression fracture is:
opts: Wedgeing of vertebra (anterior column shortened, posterior column maintained)
Bursting of posterior wall into canal
questions.exp: Compression fracture: wedgeing of vertebra (anterior column shortened, posterior column maintained). (Book p176)

questions.q: The characteristic feature of a burst fracture is:
questions.exp: Burst fracture: convex anterior and posterior walls. (Book p176)

questions.q: SCIWORA stands for:
opts: Spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality
Spinal column injury with radiographic abnormality
questions.exp: SCIWORA: spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality. (Book p177)

questions.q: In children, SCIWORA occurs because:
opts: Bone elasticity > spinal cord elasticity -> stretching of bone > spinal cord -> injury of spinal cord without fracture -> paraplegia / quadriplegia
The spinal cord is absent in children
questions.exp: In children: bone elasticity > spinal cord elasticity -> stretching of bone > spinal cord -> injury of spinal cord without fracture -> paraplegia / quadriplegia. (Book p177)

questions.q: The diagnosis of SCIWORA is made by:
questions.exp: Diagnosis: MRI. (Book p177)

questions.q: On X-ray / CT scan in SCIWORA:
questions.exp: No fracture visible on X-ray / CT scan. (Book p177)

questions.q: Spinal shock is defined as:
opts: Temporary complete cessation of functions of spinal cord below the level of injury
questions.exp: Spinal shock: temporary complete cessation of functions of spinal cord below the level of injury. (Book p177)

questions.q: The manifestations of spinal shock include all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Loss of bowel and bladder control
questions.exp: Spinal shock: anesthesia, flaccid paralysis, loss of bowel and bladder control, loss of reflex activity. (Book p177)

questions.q: The recovery time of spinal shock is:
questions.exp: Recovery time: 24-48 hours (to weeks). (Book p177)

questions.q: The first reflex to recover, marking the end of spinal shock, is the:
questions.exp: Bulbocavernosus reflex: first reflex to recover (marks end of spinal shock). (Book p177)

questions.q: The root value of the bulbocavernosus reflex is:
questions.exp: Bulbocavernosus reflex: root value: S2, S3, S4. (Book p177)

questions.q: With Foley's catheter in situ, the bulbocavernosus reflex is elicited by:
opts: Tug on catheter -> anal sphincter contracts
questions.exp: Note: if Foley's catheter in situ -> tug on catheter -> anal sphincter contracts. (Book p177)

questions.q: Neurogenic shock is:
opts: Manifestation of neurological deficits in spinal shock
questions.exp: Neurogenic shock: manifestation of neurological deficits in spinal shock. (Book p177)

questions.q: The pathophysiology of neurogenic shock begins with:
opts: Loss of sympathetic outflow -> hyperactive parasympathetic outflow
questions.exp: Pathophysiology: loss of sympathetic outflow -> hyperactive parasympathetic outflow. (Book p177)

questions.q: The cardiac feature of neurogenic shock is:
questions.exp: Loss of sympathetic outflow -> bradycardia. (Book p177)

questions.q: The blood pressure fall in neurogenic shock occurs d/t:
opts: Peripheral vasodilation -> decreased peripheral vascular resistance -> peripheral pooling of blood
questions.exp: Peripheral vasodilation -> decreased peripheral vascular resistance -> peripheral pooling of blood -> fall in BP (hypotension). (Book p177)

questions.q: In hemorrhagic shock (blood loss), the heart rate reflex is:
questions.exp: Note: in hemorrhagic shock (blood loss) -> fall in BP -> reflex tachycardia (unlike neurogenic shock's bradycardia). (Book p178)

questions.q: At birth, the spinal cord ends at the:
questions.exp: Spinal cord: at birth ends at lower border of L3. (Book p178)

questions.q: In adults, the spinal cord ends at the:
questions.exp: In adults the spinal cord ends at the upper border of L1. (Book p178)

questions.q: The plexus (bulges) of the spinal cord are:
questions.exp: Plexus (bulges): brachial (cervical region); lumbosacral. (Book p178)

questions.q: The cervical region has 7 vertebrae but:
questions.exp: Vertebral segments: cervical: 7 vertebrae, 8 nerves (thoracic 12/12, lumbar 5/5, sacral 5/5). (Book p178)

questions.q: The conus medullaris is the:
opts: Cone-shaped terminal part of the spinal cord
Bundle of nerves below the conus
questions.exp: Conus medullaris: cone-shaped terminal part of the spinal cord. (Book p178)

questions.q: The cauda equina is the:
opts: Tuft of spinal nerves below the conus
Terminal part of the spinal cord
questions.exp: Cauda equina: tuft of spinal nerves below the conus. (Book p178)

questions.q: Spinal nerve roots exit under:
opts: The transverse foramen of C1 only
questions.exp: Spinal nerve roots exit under their corresponding spinal segment pedicle. (Book p178)

questions.q: An injury to the spinal column above L1 causes:
questions.exp: Injury to spinal column: above L1: SC injury (UMNL); below L1: spinal nerve injury (LMNL). (Book p178)

questions.q: An injury to the spinal column below L1 causes:
questions.exp: Below L1: spinal nerve injury (LMNL). (Book p178)

questions.q: Above the level of injury, in both UMNL and LMNL:
questions.exp: Above the level of injury: all functions normal in both UMNL and LMNL. (Book p179)

questions.q: At the level of injury in LMNL, the motor function shows:
questions.exp: At the level of injury, LMNL: motor weakness (flaccid paralysis); reflexes absent; sensory lost. (Book p179)

questions.q: Below the level of injury in UMNL:
opts: Spastic paralysis with exaggerated reflexes and sensory loss
questions.exp: Below the level of injury, UMNL: spastic paralysis, exaggerated reflexes, sensory functions lost. (Book p179)

questions.q: Below the level of injury in LMNL:
opts: Motor normal, reflexes normal, sensory normal
questions.exp: Below the level of injury, LMNL: motor functions normal, reflexes normal, sensory normal. (Book p179)

questions.q: In UMNL there is spastic paralysis with exaggerated reflexes because:
opts: UMNL has an inhibitory action on LMNL
questions.exp: UMNL: inhibitory action on LMNL -> in UMNL: spastic paralysis with exaggerated reflexes. (Book p179)

questions.q: Each spinal nerve supplies a particular:
opts: Dermatome (cutaneous distribution), myotome (muscle groups) and reflex
questions.exp: Each spinal nerve supplies a particular dermatome (cutaneous distribution), myotome (muscle groups), reflex. (Book p179)

questions.q: A dermatome is the:
opts: Cutaneous sensory supply of spinal nerves
questions.exp: Dermatomes: cutaneous sensory supply of spinal nerves. (Book p179)

questions.q: The C5 myotome is:
questions.exp: Myotome C5: elbow flexion (biceps, brachialis). (Book p179)

questions.q: The C6 myotome is:
questions.exp: Myotome C6: wrist extension. (Book p179)

questions.q: The C7 myotome is:
questions.exp: Myotome C7: elbow extension and wrist flexion. (Book p179)

questions.q: The C8 myotome is:
questions.exp: Myotome C8: finger flexion. (Book p179)

questions.q: The T1 myotome is:
questions.exp: Myotome T1: finger abduction. (Book p179)

questions.q: The L2 myotome is:
questions.exp: Myotome L2: hip flexion / iliopsoas. (Book p179)

questions.q: The L3 myotome is:
questions.exp: Myotome L3: knee extension / quadriceps. (Book p179)

questions.q: The L4 myotome is:
questions.exp: Myotome L4: ankle dorsiflexors / tibialis anterior. (Book p179)

questions.q: The L5 myotome is:
questions.exp: Myotome L5: toe extensors / extensor hallucis longus. (Book p179)

questions.q: The S1 myotome is:
questions.exp: Myotome S1: ankle plantarflexors / gastrosoleus. (Book p179)

questions.q: The C5 reflex is the:
questions.exp: Reflex C5: biceps. (Book p180)

questions.q: The C6 reflex is the:
questions.exp: Reflex C6: supinator (brachioradialis). (Book p180)

questions.q: The C7 reflex is the:
questions.exp: Reflex C7: triceps. (Book p180)

questions.q: The L3, L4 reflex is the:
questions.exp: Reflex L3, L4: knee (quadriceps). (Book p180)

questions.q: The S1 reflex is the:
questions.exp: Reflex S1: ankle (gastrosoleus). (Book p180)

questions.q: The diaphragm receives its nerve supply from:
questions.exp: Note: diaphragm: nerve supply C3, C4, C5; injury above C3 -> affects breathing. (Book p180)

units.title: Spine: Components & Anatomy
units.guide: The spine is musculoskeletal (vertebral column) and neurological (cord plus roots). Four zones of vertebrae - cervical, thoracic/dorsal, lumbar, sacral - are joined by discs of annulus fibrosus and nucleus pulposus that segment the spine for mobility and absorb shock. Fracture the pars inter-articularis and it is spondylolysis; let it slip and spondylolisthesis follows, while the articular facets keep the spine aligned.

units.title: Denis' Concept of Stability
units.guide: Denis splits the vertebra into three columns: anterior (anterior longitudinal ligament, anterior annulus, anterior 2/3rd of body), middle (posterior 1/3rd of body, posterior annulus, posterior longitudinal ligament) and posterior (pedicles, facets, lamina, spinous process with posterior ligaments). One column hurt means stable and conservative; two or more columns down means unstable and it goes to fixation surgery.

units.title: Trauma to Spine
units.guide: Fractures cluster at T12; dislocations haunt the cervical spine, where ligamentous stabilizers outweigh bony ones and the facets sit horizontally. In the lumbar region the vertical facets favour fracture over dislocation - and a cervical fracture carries the highest spinal cord injury risk. First aid: onto the back, support behind the neck, transport to the nearest hospital.

units.title: Jefferson's Fracture
units.guide: Jefferson's fracture - the m/c C1 (atlas) fracture - is axial loading bursting fragments outward away from the canal, so neurological deficits are spared. The open-mouth view and CT (best) display it; a stable ring is treated conservatively, while a torn transverse ligament demands atlanto-occipital fusion.

units.title: C2: Odontoid & Hangman's
units.guide: C2 fractures are odontoid (the m/c of C2) or Hangman's - a fracture of the C2 pars inter-articularis, spondylolysis of C2, that lets C2 dislocate over C3. Despite the violence, the cord usually spares the patient neurological deficit; RTA tops hanging as the m/c cause.

units.title: Whiplash & Clay Shoveler's
units.guide: Whiplash is a soft tissue snap - hyperextension into flexion - leaving chronic neck pain with no deficits and normal X-ray/CT; a cervical collar settles it. Clay Shoveler's is the muscular twin: a shoveller's strong paraspinal and upper limb contraction avulses the C7 spinous process.

units.title: Chance Fracture
units.guide: Dr. G.G. Chance's seat-belt (jack-knife) fracture is a complete transverse split - bony Chance through the vertebra, soft tissue Chance through ligament and disc. A lap belt without shoulder harness flexes the lumbar spine, transecting the cord through all three columns: an unstable fracture that paraplegises and demands stabilization and surgery.

units.title: Compression vs Burst Fractures
units.guide: Compression fractures are osteoporosis's flexion-compression wedge: the anterior column shortens, the posterior column holds. Burst fractures are significant trauma's axial loading: the anterior and posterior walls both bow convex. Different villains, different films.

units.title: SCIWORA
units.guide: SCIWORA - spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality - is the child's privilege of pliable bone: bone elasticity exceeds cord elasticity, the bone stretches, the cord does not, and paraplegia or quadriplegia arrives with no fracture on X-ray or CT. Only MRI confesses the injury.

units.title: Spinal Shock
units.guide: Spinal shock is the temporary complete cessation of spinal cord function below the injury: anesthesia, flaccid paralysis, lost bowel and bladder control, silent reflexes. Recovery takes 24-48 hours to weeks, and the bulbocavernosus reflex - S2, S3, S4, elicited by tugging the Foley catheter till the anal sphincter contracts - is the first to return, marking the shock's end.

units.title: Neurogenic Shock
units.guide: Neurogenic shock is the circulatory arm of spinal shock: loss of sympathetic outflow unleashes hyperactive parasympathetic tone, the heart bradycardias, vessels dilate, resistance falls, blood pools peripherally and pressure sinks. Contrast it with hemorrhagic shock, where blood loss buys a reflex tachycardia instead.

units.title: Spinal Cord Anatomy
units.guide: The cord climbs with the child: ending at the lower border of L3 at birth, it retreats to the upper border of L1 in the adult, throwing up brachial and lumbosacral bulges. Seven cervical vertebrae serve eight nerve pairs (thoracic and sacral twelve and five each); the cone-shaped conus medullaris caps the cord while the cauda equina tuft of roots drifts below, each root exiting under its own segment's pedicle.

units.title: UMNL vs LMNL
units.guide: L1 is the watershed: above it, cord (UMNL); below it, roots (LMNL). Above the lesion everything is normal either way; at the level, LMNL flaccidises with absent reflexes; below, UMNL spasms with exaggerated reflexes while LMNL keeps functioning normally - because the UMNL's inhibitory hand on the LMNL has been removed.

units.title: Dermatomes & Myotomes
units.guide: Every root owns a dermatome of skin, a myotome of muscle and a reflex. The myotome ladder runs C5 elbow flexion, C6 wrist extension, C7 elbow extension with wrist flexion, C8 finger flexion, T1 finger abduction, then L2 hip flexion, L3 knee extension, L4 ankle dorsiflexion, L5 toe extension, S1 ankle plantarflexion.

units.title: Reflexes & Diaphragm
units.guide: The reflex map: C5 biceps, C6 supinator (brachioradialis), C7 triceps, L3-L4 knee, S1 ankle. And the diaphragm breathes on C3, C4, C5 - an injury above C3 endangers the breath itself.
